questions.q: Explain opportunity cost with an example.
questions.m: It's the highest-valued alternative you give up. If you spend an evening studying rather than working a paid shift, the wage you gave up is the opportunity cost.

questions.q: Explain the difference between positive and normative statements.
questions.m: Positive statements say what is and can be tested against facts. Normative statements say what ought to be and rest on value judgments.

questions.q: Explain the difference between comparative and absolute advantage.
questions.m: Comparative advantage is producing at a lower opportunity cost. Absolute advantage is being more productive, producing more with the same resources.

questions.q: Explain how specialization makes both Liz and Joe better off.
questions.m: Each specializes in the good with a lower opportunity cost and then trades. Both consume combinations outside their own PPFs, gaining 5 smoothies and 5 salads each hour.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a change in demand and a change in quantity demanded.
questions.m: A change in the good's own price causes a change in quantity demanded, a movement along the curve. A change in any other factor causes a change in demand, a shift of the whole curve.

questions.q: Explain how a shortage returns a market to equilibrium.
questions.m: At a price below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. Buyers bid up the price, which raises quantity supplied and lowers quantity demanded until they are equal.

questions.q: A drought hits date farms. What happens to price and quantity, and why?
questions.m: The state of nature reduces supply, shifting it leftward. The equilibrium price rises and the quantity falls.

questions.q: Explain the total revenue test.
questions.m: If a price rise reduces total revenue, demand is elastic. If it raises total revenue, demand is inelastic. If revenue doesn't change, demand is unit elastic.

questions.q: Explain why a competitive market is efficient.
questions.m: At equilibrium marginal benefit equals marginal cost, so every unit worth more than it costs is produced and none worth less. Total surplus is maximized.

questions.q: Explain deadweight loss with underproduction.
questions.m: When less than the efficient quantity is produced, marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost for the missing units. The surplus those units would have created is lost.

questions.q: Explain how to find the taxed quantity and prices using demand and supply equations.
questions.m: Set the demand price minus the supply price equal to the tax, solve for Q, then substitute Q into the demand equation for the buyers' price and into the supply equation for the sellers' price.

questions.q: Explain how elasticity determines tax incidence.
questions.m: The side that is less able to respond pays more. More inelastic demand puts more of the tax on buyers, and more inelastic supply puts more of it on sellers.

questions.q: Explain the paradox of value.
questions.m: Water has a large total utility but a small marginal utility because we consume so much. Diamonds have a small total utility but a large marginal utility. Price reflects marginal utility, so water is cheap.

questions.q: Explain why a fall in a good's price increases the quantity demanded.
questions.m: A lower price raises that good's marginal utility per riyal above the other good's. The consumer buys more of it until the ratios are equal again, so the quantity demanded rises and the demand curve slopes down.

questions.q: Explain the MR = MC rule.
questions.m: If producing one more unit adds more to revenue than to cost, profit rises, so produce more. If it adds more to cost than revenue, produce less. Profit is maximized where MR equals MC.

questions.q: How do you tell whether a firm makes a profit, breaks even or makes a loss?
questions.m: Compare price with ATC at the profit-maximizing output: P > ATC means profit, P = ATC means break even, and P < ATC means a loss.

questions.q: Explain why marginal revenue is less than price for a monopoly.
questions.m: To sell one more unit the monopoly must lower the price on every unit. The extra unit adds its price, but revenue is lost on units that were sold at the higher price, so MR is below price.

questions.q: Name the three types of barrier to entry, with an example of each.
questions.m: Natural, from economies of scale, such as an electricity supplier. Ownership of a key resource, such as diamond mines. Legal, such as a public franchise or a patent.

questions.q: Explain what happens in the long run when firms make economic profits.
questions.m: The profit attracts new firms. Each existing firm's demand decreases until price equals ATC and firms only break even.

questions.q: Compare monopolistic competition with perfect competition and monopoly.
questions.m: Like perfect competition it has many firms and free entry, so profit doesn't last. Like monopoly each firm faces a downward-sloping demand and sets price. Products are differentiated rather than identical or unique.
